text:
#News Voters are saying they walked into polling places only to find that a ballot had already been cast under their name.

A couple of examples:

🔴Jean Franco Urbaez said he showed up to the Church of the Good Shepherd in Lower Macungie Township to vote in person.

➡️Instead, he found an electronic check-in record showing someone had already voted using his identity at 8:11 a.m.

➡️He started recording until poll workers told him to stop.

“At 8:11 a.m. this morning, someone else went IN PERSON to my local polling place and stole my vote. They forged my signature and were able to cast a ballot in my name because we don’t ask for VOTER ID. To make matters worse, the ONLY form of verification we apparently ask for in PA is your street address?"

"So, did I have to provide my street address? No! They provided it to me. All you have to say is, ‘Yep, that’s me,’ and boom, you get to vote.”

➡️Poll workers offered him a provisional ballot. He accepted, noting that whether his provisional vote counts would depend on later review of the earlier signature and the claim that he was not the person who checked in while he was still at home.

🔴In Northern Virginia the same day, Fox News contributor Kaylee McGhee White and her husband showed up to their polling place and said:

“Just voted in commie NoVa. Showed up, checked in, were immediately told a mail-in ballot had already been submitted for my husband. I cannot overstate how important it is to show up today. This would not have been caught if we had not gone in person.”
Other reports:

🔷️Early-voting “ballot switching” reports in Tennessee, South Carolina, Texas, Florida, and Ohio.
🔷️Voters posted that touchscreen machines selected a Democrat when they selected a Republican.
🔷️Duplicate mail ballots: Tulare County, California, mailed 7,791 extra ballots because of a vendor error.
🔷️Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, sent about 150–157 duplicates because of human error.

How many more people had a ballot cast in their name when they didn’t even vote or planned to vote in person?

text:
Republicans didn't just lose the midterms on Tuesday. They got evicted. Democrats took the House and the Senate in a wave that reached deep into red country. Texas elected its first Democratic senator since 1988, and the Washington Post called it the largest shift to the left in half a century.
Faced with a verdict that loud, Trump did what he always does: he went looking for someone to carry the blame. Leviticus has a word for this. Aaron laid the sins of Israel on a goat and sent it into the wilderness. Trump's goat was Susie Wiles, and her wilderness has a payroll.
Wiles is the operator who got him back into the White House, and by most accounts she was one of the few moderating forces in his second term. On Wednesday Trump said nobody would be fired over the results. By Friday nobody had been, technically. Wiles had resigned. According to Axios, Trump spent the days after the election unable to shake the idea that she was to blame, not him. She offered to quit, offered again, and made it official Thursday night. Trump accepted, thanked her for an "outstanding job," and announced she'd be "moving over to the Trump Political Operation." That's the same operation whose midterm spending he'd reportedly been grousing about. Her replacement, starting Monday, is Stephen Miller.
Now look at who didn't get blamed.
Pete Hegseth has been the face of the Iran war for eight months. He's the man who declared a "capital 'V'" victory back in April. Since then fuel prices have climbed and voters have blamed the war for them. The war also broke the "no new wars" pitch Trump ran on. His own vice president said it plainest the morning after: "The reason we lost is the war." Trump himself admitted the war cost them. Then, asked whether Hegseth was safe, he said his defense secretary was "doing a very good job." Asked about the war itself: "If I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again." That isn't a defense. It's a diagnosis.
Miller is the architect of the mass-deportation campaign. It was sold as a hunt for the "worst of the worst." It ended up sweeping up long-settled residents, workers, and people with no criminal record. It also helped give back the Latino gains Trump made in 2024. In Texas, roughly seven in ten Hispanic voters backed Democrat James Talarico for Senate. Democrats won every House district on the U.S.–Mexico border for the first time since 2008. Prices and the war did plenty of damage too. But the enforcement machine is the part with Miller's name on it.
So the chief of staff gets moved to the campaign shop. The war's chief salesman gets a vote of confidence. And the man who designed the other policy that sank them gets the keys to the West Wing. That's not a course correction. It's doubling down on a losing hand and firing the dealer.
The pattern is older than this election. When the facts won't bend to the story, Trump removes whoever keeps delivering the facts, keeps or promotes whoever wrote the policy, and starts telling everyone else what they actually saw. It worked, after a fashion, with January 6: years of insistence talked much of his base out of what it had watched on live television. He started again on election night, telling the New York Times that Republicans lost largely because he wasn't on the ballot.
Whether that trick works on a midterm wipeout is another question. This one was driven by an unpopular war and a deportation machine running through voters' own neighborhoods. A riot can be argued over for years. A gas bill shows up every month. Still, the first personnel moves make the plan plain enough. The fever isn't breaking. It's being promoted.

text:
At the 33rd Annual Baron Investment Conference, Elon Musk laid out a staggering goal for Terafab: produce 1 terawatt of AI-chip capacity every year 🔥

His argument is that even without a geopolitical crisis disrupting semiconductor supplies, the world simply isn’t making chips fast enough 🔥

By his estimates, global AI-chip production will reach approximately 20–25 gigawatts in 2026, rising to 35–45 gigawatts in 2027, depending on whose projections you believe.

Terafab’s target is 1,000 gigawatts annually—a scale he described as roughly 30 times next year’s projected global production. Those gigawatt figures represent the combined power capacity of the AI chips manufactured each year.

The name reflects that ambition: T-E-R-A, as in terawatt. Elon joked that “terror” and “terra”, meaning Earth, offer other interpretations. Given the size of the undertaking, he suggested all three might apply. It is, in his words, “terrifyingly large”.

When Ron Baron compared one plant’s potential output with the GDP of the twentieth-largest country, Elon suggested it might even make the top ten. It was a speculative comparison, but it gives you a sense of how big he’s thinking.

The price tag could be just as extraordinary. Ron suggested $1 trillion, and Elon replied, “Probably more than that.” Construction would happen in phases, spreading out the capital requirements as the project develops.

Elon believes it will succeed, at least to some degree. He also acknowledged how much the outcome will shape people’s judgment: if it fails, it will look crazy; if it succeeds, it will look audacious.

Part of his plan for getting there involves rethinking what happens inside a chip factory. According to Elon, a wafer can spend more than half its time being transported or waiting for equipment. In some cases, useful changes to its atoms happen during only about 20% of its time inside the fab.

The wafers can be zipping around the building while spending relatively little time undergoing useful processing. That gap is where he sees a major opportunity to improve manufacturing efficiency.

So why haven’t established chipmakers already overhauled the process? His explanation comes down to the enormous capital tied to a working recipe. Once a fab reliably produces chips, trying something radically different puts expensive production at risk. Proven methods and incremental improvements become the safer business decision.

His plan creates room for experimentation through a research fab at Gigafactory Texas in Austin. The facility would test different approaches to semiconductor manufacturing, with the expectation that many will fail and some will work.

The successful approaches would then move into the production Terafab in Grimes County, Texas, near Texas A&M, where those improvements could be scaled.

At the Austin research facility, logic, memory, packaging, and lithography capabilities would come together under one roof. That would support a much tighter cycle of designing a chip, making it, testing it, and feeding the results into the next version.

His ambition is to shrink a development cycle that normally takes a year to approximately a month. Every faster cycle creates another opportunity to discover what works, fix what doesn’t, and improve the process before scaling it.

That speed is central to the whole approach. In Elon’s view, technological progress depends on two things: how many iterations you can complete and how much improvement you achieve between them.

His rule of thumb is powerful: if you can iterate an order of magnitude faster, then, as a first approximation, you can advance the technology an order of magnitude faster 💡

text:
America Is Digging Its Own
Grave for Mammon

A nation does not have to be conquered to lose its freedom. It can surrender it willingly, one election, one institution, and one generation at a time. What we are watching is people voting to commit cultural suicide for the promise of more money in their pockets.

The November 3, 2026, midterm elections exposed a country in far deeper trouble than another disappointing Republican election cycle. Ungodly leftists were voted in, and the demonic Democrats captured the House and Senate.

Eight Democratic Socialists of America (i.e., Communists/Marxists/Socialists) won U.S. House seats in the 2026 midterms: incumbents Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib, along with newcomers Chris Rabb, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Darializa Avila-Chevalier, Claire Valdez, and Angela Gonzales-Torres. Who would ever think these types of people would be voted for in our system of government?

We saw Abdul El-Sayed, whose family is friendly with the Muslim Brotherhood, win in Michigan and become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. This brings the total to 256 Muslims in elected office throughout the United States, according to CAIR. Can you believe this? Talk about a takeover!

We saw Chris Pappas of New Hampshire win a U.S. Senate seat, becoming the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. That brings the total to 1,359 openly LGBTQ+ elected officials serving nationwide, across federal, state, and local government, according to the LGBTQ+ Victory Institute.

We saw a Christian apostate, James Talarico, win in Texas. He believes God is nonbinary, that Scripture does not establish a single Christian position against abortion or gay marriage, and that salvation is works-based, wrongly invoking the sheep and goat judgment in Matthew 25. Can it get any worse?

We watched Texas flip—the buckle of the Bible Belt handed to the Left. If that can happen in a longtime Republican and Christian stronghold, we cannot afford to take any state for granted.

Americans handed the radical Left power, and the consequences will extend well beyond what you and I can imagine.

This Is Not About Political Messaging

I am tired of hearing that every political catastrophe is merely a messaging problem. I’ve heard this from many talking heads, pundits, and podcasters. On one level, I get it. If we are just talking about politics, I understand that argument. Trump and the Republicans failed big time in explaining to people what was going on with Iran, economics, and other pertinent items. But it’s more than that. Way more.

Some Voters Simply Stayed Home; Now We All Pay the Price.

According to University of Florida election researcher Michael McDonald, 50.6% of eligible voters did not vote. Being too lazy to vote is a surrender of responsibility. If you cannot be bothered to cast a ballot, you leave others to choose the leaders, laws, and policies that will shape your life and your children’s future. The election proceeds without you, and those who vote choose the government we all must live under. Complaining about the country while refusing to participate in its elections is hollow. Staying home does not shield you from the consequences; it gives you less say in the decisions that produce them.

Furthermore, I would never sit out an election as a way of punishing Trump or the Republicans for not satisfying my economic desires, or offer a pietistic excuse that politics is simply too dirty for the heavenly minded. Look, Mr. Pietist: when you don’t vote, you leave the decision to those who do—and you still have to live with the consequences. Don’t you get it?  When you don’t vote, you’re essentially giving the worst candidate your vote. You’re not punishing Trump or the Republicans as you think; your non-vote is allowing a radical to come in and dismantle America.  You’re to blame for this! Who thinks like this? Who acts like this? Oh, that’s right: people who don’t understand how our political system works, and those elections have consequences we all have to live with.  So, thanks to everyone who couldn’t be bothered to vote: now we all must live with the mess your inaction helped create…

text:
AN OPEN LETTER TO JAMES TALARICO AND GINA HINOJOSA
You made a lot of promises to the people of Texas. Now comes the part that matters: delivering on them.
Gina, I want to remind you of what you are inheriting.
Texas is an extraordinary state. Not because of one politician, one political party, or one election, but because of generations of hardworking Texans who built something worth protecting.
Texas has earned a reputation as an economic powerhouse.
Consider what this state has accomplished:
* Texas has received the Governor’s Cup from Site Selection magazine for attracting major business investment projects year after year.
* Texas has repeatedly been recognized for its business climate and economic development.
* Texas has no individual state income tax.
* Texas is home to major industries in energy, technology, aerospace, manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare.
* Texas is a national leader in energy production.
* Texas has attracted major corporate headquarters, manufacturing facilities, and business expansions.
* Texas has one of the largest state economies in America.
* Texas has experienced tremendous population growth as people and businesses seek opportunity here.
* Texas has a long tradition of entrepreneurship, independence, and private investment.
And those accomplishments didn’t happen by accident.
They happened because people worked, invested, took risks, built businesses, created jobs, and believed in the opportunities this state offered.
You are not inheriting a state that needs to be torn down and rebuilt. You are inheriting a state with an extraordinary foundation.
That doesn’t mean Texas is perfect. We have serious challenges involving property taxes, education, infrastructure, water, healthcare, and affordability.
There is plenty of work to do.
So please, don’t become another politician who makes promises, wins an election, and spends the next four years making excuses.
Protect what works. Fix what doesn’t. And make Texas even better than you found it.
And James, I have a similar message for you.
Go be the person you told Texans you would be.
Will you reach across party lines and work for the people you represent, including those who didn’t vote for you?
Will you evaluate legislation based on whether it benefits Texans rather than which political party introduced it?
Will you put meaningful results ahead of political theater?
And when Washington becomes consumed with partisan investigations, impeachment debates, and political battles, will you demand evidence, accountability, and responsible use of taxpayer dollars?
Those are fair questions, and Texans deserve answers.
Regardless of how anyone feels about the president, Congress has a responsibility to evaluate policies, investigate legitimate concerns, protect constitutional principles, and use taxpayer resources wisely.
We should expect our elected officials to distinguish between legitimate oversight and political gamesmanship.
The great coach Nick Saban has often emphasized the importance of discipline, preparation, and controlling emotions.
That’s a lesson worth remembering in politics.
Emotion should never replace sound judgment. Political outrage should never become a substitute for leadership.
The job is not to win the next argument on social media.
The job is to govern.
And to both of you, I want to say something else.
Those of us who didn’t vote for you are still Texans.
We still own businesses, employ people, pay taxes, raise families, volunteer in our communities, and contribute to the economy.
We aren’t going anywhere.
We aren’t obligated to agree with you, but we are entitled to expect you to represent us.
We don’t have to march in the streets, organize protests, or spend our days attacking people on social media to make our voices matter.
We will continue doing what Texans have always done.
We will work. We will build. We will invest. We will raise our families. We will help our neighbors.
And we will pay attention.
Because winning an election is not the accomplishment. What you do after winning is what defines your leadership.
So here’s my challenge to both of you:
Keep your promises.
Work across party lines.
Respect the taxpayers.
Protect the opportunities that made Texas successful.
Address the problems that genuinely need fixing.
And remember that you represent every Texan, not just the ones who voted for you.
Texas was great before you took office. Your responsibility is to leave it better than you found it.
Save this post.
Let’s revisit it in a year. And again in four years.
Not to measure your speeches, your social media following, or how many political opponents you’ve criticized.
But to measure your actual results.
We are watching. We are paying attention. And we expect you to deliver.
Don’t let Texas down! See less

text:
STMICRO $STM STILL TRADES LIKE AN AI CHIP STOCK:

STMicroelectronics (STM) at $41.72, +$1.77 / +4.43% on Friday.

STMicroelectronics stays off every Len5 we weigh except Quality, and a lower price changes none of that before its December quarter is reported. Thursday's chip selloff, with no news from the company, took it to its lowest close since April and pulled Texas Instruments down nearly as far, which erases the line our post drew between STMicroelectronics's AI chips and its factory and car chips. Friday's rebound put it back with the AI chip makers, and it has moved almost step for step with a fund of the largest chip makers since its October 29 report.

STMicroelectronics is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es, and it still passes the Quality Len5: a profit over the first nine months of 2026, with debt under a fifth of the owners' stake. Quality-Value wants a durable profit at a discount, and the price half now clears the $52.16 ceiling our post set by $10.44. The profit half has not moved since the October 29 report. What would put it on the Quality-Value Len5: a December-quarter profit replacing last year's loss when the past four quarters are added up, reported January 28 before the US open. Deep-Value and Special-Situations wants a price well under a cautious value of the cash the business makes, and September's free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and paying for plants, was $351 million. Four quarters at that pace would bring in about 3.5 cents a year for each dollar of the share price, too thin for that Len5 even after this week. What would put it on the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5: that pace held for a full year at a price well under this one. Momentum wants months of gains near a high, and Friday's close sits 48.8% under the June 3 peak; months of gains that win back much of that fall would put it on the Momentum Len5. Income wants cash paid to owners with room to spare, and the dividend is under 1% of the price; a payout several times larger would put it on the Income Len5. Hypergrowth wants sales multiplying, and September-quarter sales grew 17.9%; sales doubling from a year earlier would put it on the Hypergrowth Len5.

Thursday took STMicroelectronics to $39.95, its lowest close since April 10, on no news from the company.
- Thursday: -$5.65 / -12.39%, its steepest one-day fall since July 23.
- VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) at $463.96, +$16.23 / +3.62% on Friday. Thursday: -11.21%.
- Texas Instruments (TXN) at $277.36, -$0.79 / -0.28% on Friday. Thursday: -10.70%.
The VanEck fund holds the largest US-listed chip makers. A Thursday-morning report from Investing, the market-news site, tied the chip selling to worry that a Democratic Congress will bring stricter rules on building data centers. Texas Instruments, the Dallas maker of chips for factories, cars and electronics, has fallen further than STMicroelectronics since Wednesday's close:
- STMicroelectronics: -$3.88 / -8.5%.
- Chip fund: -$40.31 / -8.0%.
- Texas Instruments: -$34.13 / -11.0%.
Our post had Texas Instruments coming through the selling higher, spared by its factory and car chips. Our premise was faulty: we treated those chips as the part of the market the AI selling would skip, and Thursday's sellers did not skip them. Texas Instruments is on none of the Len5es we weigh; at about 36 times the past year's profit, it offers the value Len5es no discount.

Friday split the two again. STMicroelectronics rose 4.43%, ahead of the chip fund, while Texas Instruments slipped. From the October 29 close, report day:
- STMicroelectronics: -$8.27 / -16.5%.
- Chip fund: -$97.71 / -17.4%.
- Texas Instruments: -$35.58 / -11.4%.
The chip fund's largest holdings sell chips for AI data centers, and STMicroelectronics has stayed within a point of it since the report, falling harder on Thursday and bouncing harder on Friday. We called that right. Our read: investors price STMicroelectronics on its data-center chips, and the factory and car chips that make up most of its sales follow.

A quarter that cleared every bar we set has left STMicroelectronics $3.67 under where our first post found it on October 16, and still off every Len5 but Quality. Factory and car chips did not shield Texas Instruments on Thursday, and they have not shielded STMicroelectronics since October 29, with nothing due from the company before January 28.

text:
STMICRO $STM CLEARED OUR BAR, THEN FELL 9%:

STMicroelectronics (STM) at $45.60, -$2.94 / -6.06% on Wednesday, and $45.00 premarket, -$0.60 / -1.32% from that close.

STMicroelectronics stays off every Len5 we weigh, and the October 29 report moved the profit half of the Quality-Value test we set without closing it. The company cleared every bar our post set, including a $4.15 billion fourth-quarter forecast. The shares rose 3% that day, then fell further than the makers of everyday chips on two days of selling that came from Intel and from Washington, and the stock is lower than when we wrote while they are higher, the AI-bet call our post made. We called it. Our premise on NXP was faulty: its after-hours fall was not the market's verdict. The data-center line, now nine cents of each sales dollar, is the part of the company that traded on both days.

STMicroelectronics is not on the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es, and it still passes the Quality Len5 on its books: a $550 million profit over nine months, with $3.21 billion of debt under $17.88 billion of owners' equity. Quality-Value wants a durable profit at a discount, and our post set its test: profit closing the gap to 2024 at a price under $52.16. The price half holds. The profit half moved: the past four quarters earned $520 million, from $466 million when we wrote, against $1.56 billion in 2024. What would put it on the Quality-Value Len5: a December-quarter profit on the $4.15 billion of sales it forecast, replacing last year's $30 million loss in the four-quarter count, with the shares still under $52.16. Momentum wants months of gains near the high, and the shares are 44% under the June 3 high. Deep-Value and Special-Situations wants a sound business under a cautious value of the cash it produces; the quarter's $351 million of free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and paying for plants, follows a first half that spent more than it brought in, and a year at that pace at a lower price would put it on that Len5. Income wants cash paid to owners with room to spare, and Hypergrowth a young business multiplying its sales; a 0.7% dividend from a company founded in 1987 is neither.

The October 29 report cleared the three bars we set: revenue against its own midpoint, the gross margin, what the company keeps of each sales dollar after making the chips, against 37%, and the fourth-quarter forecast against $4 billion.
- Revenue $3.76B, +17.9%; gross margin 37.3%, from 33.2%; profit $291M, from $237M.
- Adjusted profit, with restructuring costs stripped out: $0.37 a share against about $0.40 expected, the one miss.
- October-December forecast: revenue $4.15B at the midpoint, plus or minus 3.5%, so the low end also clears $4B; gross margin about 39%.
Jean-Marc Chery, its chief executive, said "demand remains well above supply."

The shares got one day for it. They closed October 29 at their highest since October 12 and are now 8.8% under that close, after two falls on days when nothing from the company moved the price.
- October 29, report day: $49.99, +$1.47 / +3.03%.
- October 30: $46.74, -$3.25 / -6.50%. Intel (INTC) at $58.27, -$2.28 / -3.77% on Wednesday, had forecast December-quarter revenue short of estimates and fell 28.6% that day. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) at $504.27, -$14.25 / -2.75% on Wednesday, lost 6.98%.
- November 4: $45.60, -$2.94 / -6.06%, with nothing from the company but new microcontrollers. Texas Instruments (TXN) at $311.49, -$1.00 / -0.32% on Wednesday, barely moved, and NXP rose.
- Since our post: STMicroelectronics -$3.08 / -6.3%; the chip fund -9.6%; Texas Instruments +0.8%.
Our read: Wednesday's sellers, who dumped the AI data-center suppliers after Democrats won both houses of Congress, counted STMicroelectronics among them, not among the makers of everyday chips for factories and cars; it fell twice as far as the chip fund. Intel is on none of the Len5es we weigh; it lost money over the past year. Texas Instruments is on none either, at about 40 times profit.

NXP Semiconductors (NXPI) at $265.01, +$2.22 / +0.84% on Wednesday, is where our premise was faulty. We wrote that its 7.6% after-hours fall, to $234.25, showed what a forecast half a percent short costs. By the next close the cost was 0.7%.
- October 28: $251.69, -$1.81 / -0.71%. October 29: $266.00, +$14.31 / +5.69%.
NXP is +$11.51 / +4.5% since our post, and it is on none of the Len5es we weigh: about 21 times the past year's profit after a forecast under estimates is neither a discount nor Momentum's climb.

Our post put the data-center line at seven cents of each sales dollar; by the company's figures it is now nine. It expects about $1.3 billion of AI data-center revenue this year, up from the $1 billion it named in June. Most of it is silicon photonics, chips that move data as light, and microcontrollers. Chery said that revenue would be "well above doubling" in 2027.
- RF and optical communications, the product line holding the data-center chips: $504M in the quarter, +46.2%, against +17.9% for the whole company.
Those nine cents are what the market sold on October 30 and again on Wednesday; the other 91 cents, the factory and car chips Texas Instruments and NXP also sell, left both of those companies higher than when we wrote.

January 28, 2027, before the US open, STMicroelectronics reports the December quarter against its own $4.15 billion and 39%, with the 2027 data-center figure Chery promised. Its Paris shares: 40.03 euros, -0.86 euros / -2.09% at 11:51am Paris time, by MarketScreener's count. Our first post found this stock at $45.39 on October 16; a reported quarter and a $4.15 billion forecast later, it is 21 cents higher.

text:
Amouranth posted a screenshot showing $20 million in Bitcoin and asked her followers if she should sell. A few months later, three masked men shot open her bedroom door, put a gun to her head and asked one question: “Where’s the crypto?” What she did next put one of them in the hospital, and that’s not even the strangest part.

In the video below, she and her husband sit down and walk through the whole night.

It was March 2, 2025, around 11 p.m., at her home in Houston. She was going to bed early when she heard loud bangs downstairs. Her husband was in a separate building on the property, and when she called him, he was on the toilet. He told her it was probably the dogs. She locked her door anyway.

A few minutes later the men shot the door open, turned on the lights and pushed her into a chair. They kept asking for the crypto. When she said she didn’t know how to hand over digital money, one of them said “hit her,” and they pistol-whipped her three times.

Then she realized her phone call had never ended. Her husband had heard everything on speakerphone.

So she lied. She said she knew exactly where the crypto was and offered to take them to it. She led all three across the property, straight to the building where her husband was. He later admitted he didn’t even stop to wipe. He grabbed his gun, put on a bulletproof vest and waited by the stairs. As she came around the corner, he told her to duck and fired. One of the men screamed that he’d been shot, and all three ran.

The only thing they got away with was her MacBook. When she checked its location, it was in the same hospital where doctors were treating her head wounds. She thinks she may have passed the man who was shot on her way out.

Days later, troopers pulled a car over for not using its turn signal and found a partly cleaned bloodstain in the back seat. The driver confessed. Four teenagers, the youngest just 16, were charged with aggravated kidnapping and aggravated robbery, which in Texas can carry up to 99 years.

Would you have handed over the crypto, or done what she did?

text:
I'm concerned that conservatives are being lulled into a false sense of security about what happened Tuesday, especially those of us living in states that are still comfortably Republican.

Oklahoma stayed red. Republicans kept their statewide offices and their legislative supermajority. Yet Democrats flipped six seats in the Oklahoma House, made substantial gains in our largest counties, and came within roughly 3,300 votes of winning a congressional race.

I've been watching what's happening in other states, particularly Texas, and I think we're underestimating how quickly the political landscape can change.

There's something happening right here in Tulsa that I've been concerned about for years.

It's called Tulsa Remote, although I've privately referred to it as Turn Tulsa Blue.

For those unfamiliar with the program, Tulsa Remote was launched in 2018 with funding from the George Kaiser Family Foundation. It recruits people who already have jobs they can perform remotely and offers them $10,000 to relocate to Tulsa.

From an economic development standpoint, it sounds fantastic. Tulsa gains residents who bring outside income into the local economy, rent or purchase homes, shop at local businesses, and contribute to the tax base. Their employers don't even have to be located in Oklahoma.

The people moving here receive $10,000, a relatively affordable place to live, and assistance getting established in a new city. It's easy to understand why the program receives so much positive attention.

What many people probably don't realize is how much further the program goes.

Tulsa Remote actively helps participants build relationships through organized social events, networking opportunities, volunteer programs, nonprofits, and civic organizations. Research on the program has even documented introductions to local school boards.

Take a look at its own Community Resources directory.

It has an entire section devoted to "Social Justice," directing newcomers toward organizations involved in advocacy and public policy. Among those listed are Oklahomans for Equality, the Terence Crutcher Foundation, ACTION Tulsa, and Tulsa Global Alliance.

Other sections introduce people to Black Queer Tulsa, Twisted Arts, and the Oklahoma Equality Center Health Clinic.

These organizations have their own priorities and advocacy efforts, some involving LGBTQ issues, racial justice, and broader progressive social policies. These are issues that directly influence the cultural and political direction of a community.

What I'd particularly like to know is how much of Tulsa Remote's organized community involvement flows toward these groups compared with organizations representing different perspectives.

More than 4,000 people have participated in Tulsa Remote since the program began, and it reports that approximately 80% remain after two years.

Years ago, I had a conversation with someone who worked with Tulsa Remote in its early stages. That person described it to me as an undercover effort to turn Tulsa blue.

I've never forgotten that conversation.

George Kaiser's history of supporting Democratic politics, including fundraising for Barack Obama, is publicly documented. His foundation is the primary financial backer of Tulsa Remote.

Here's the part I find especially interesting.

Tulsa Remote describes its mission as helping shape Tulsa's future. When they tell you they're helping shape Tulsa's future, believe them.

They're recruiting people from outside Oklahoma, screening them VERY carefully, providing a financial incentive to move here, helping them establish permanent roots, and connecting them with progressive organizations that influence the community.

Think about how that works over 10-15 years. These newcomers become homeowners, parents, volunteers, nonprofit leaders, school board members, and potentially candidates for public office.
